title:
Geography
                          in Herodotus
author: Ancient
content:
Last modified:  Feb.
7, 1996

Some
important passages for Herodotean geography

Why
geography is integral to Herodotus' work

	The link between culture and geography:  the example of Egypt 
(
Hdt. 2.35
)

	The anecdote closing the whole work:  "soft lands make soft people"
 (
Hdt.
9.122
)

Note also the regular organization of Herodotus' descriptive
geography into sections on nature (
physis
), customs and history.

Geography
as the spatial dimension of natural forces

	The balance of natural forces is seen at the geographic center of the
earth:  
Hdt. 1.142

	Extremes of the world illustrate extreme effects of natural forces:

	Examples of symmetry in world geography:  Scythia as opposite of Egypt

	The Scythians are the most unlearned people in the world
(
Hdt. 4.46
);  the
Egyptians are models of learning

	Herodotus has to write more at length about Egypt because of its great
monuments
 (
Hdt. 2.35
):  the one great accomplishment of the Scythians is that
they have no towns or buildings
(
Hdt. 2.46
)

	The Istros (Danube) is the largest river in the world
(
Hdt. 2.48
);  but
the Nile is bigger if you consider that it has no tributaries
(
Hdt. 2.50.1
)

	The volume of the Istros is constant year round:  Herodotus explains why
(
Hdt. 2.50.2-4

);  the Nile is unusual in flooding in the summer:  Herodotus
explains why
Note as well that there is no abstract term for
geographic or cartographic direction in ancient Greek:  "North", "South",
"East" and "West" have to be expressed in terms of active forces that operate
there such as "North wind" or "Rising of the sun."

Critique
of geographers

	A systematic critique of world geography:  

Hdt. 4.36.2 - 4.45.5

	A critical anecdote suggests the dangers of applied geography:  

Hdt. 5.49- 50

(and note that this is followed immediately by Herodotus' "correction" of
the road to Persia, 

Hdt. 5.52- 5.54
)
